notes.text: Brown the kofta in two batches so they have room in the pan. Keep the first batch warm on a plate under foil.

move.title: Mix, squeeze, shape
move.body: Kofta are little logs of spiced ground meat, cooked all over Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, and beyond. Today you'll grate an onion and squeeze it dry, mix it into ground lamb with herbs, spices, and breadcrumbs, and shape the mixture by hand so it holds together in the pan. They're served in warm pita with a cool yogurt and mint sauce.

why.title: Mixing makes it sticky
why.body: Ground meat has proteins that turn sticky when you mix it well. Knead the mixture with your hands for a minute or two and it goes from loose crumbs to one tacky mass. That stickiness is what holds a kofta together when it cooks.

why.title: Squeeze the onion dry
why.body: Grated onion gives kofta flavor all the way through, but it's full of juice. Left in, that juice turns the mixture wet and slippery, and the kofta fall apart. Squeezing it in a towel takes out the water and keeps the flavor.

why.title: Crumbs hold the juice
why.body: Breadcrumbs are a binder. They soak up the juice the lamb lets go of as it cooks and keep it inside the kofta, so they stay tender and don't crumble.

why.title: Wet hands, smooth logs
why.body: Ground meat sticks to dry hands. Dip your hands in cold water and the mixture slides into a smooth log with no cracks. A log with no cracks holds together when you turn it.

why.title: Brown, then turn
why.body: A kofta sticks to the pan at first, then lets go once its side has browned. Turn it a quarter turn at a time with the tongs, so every side gets a brown crust and the middle cooks through.

wrong.sign: The kofta fall apart in the pan
wrong.fix: The mixture was too wet or not mixed enough. Knead the rest a little longer, and add a spoonful of breadcrumbs.

wrong.sign: They stick and tear when you turn them
wrong.fix: Wait another minute. A browned side lets go by itself.

wrong.sign: The outside is dark but the middle isn't at 160°F yet
wrong.fix: Turn the heat down to medium and cook 2 more minutes, turning them, before checking again.
Stir in a spoonful of water or lemon juice.

quiz.q: Why do you squeeze the grated onion?
choices: Its juice makes the mixture too wet to hold together
quiz.explain: The flavor stays; the water goes.

choices: Kneading the meat until sticky, plus the breadcrumbs
quiz.explain: The sticky meat and the crumbs are the binders.

quiz.q: What temperature does ground lamb need to reach?
quiz.explain: Ground lamb and ground beef both need 160°F.

substitutions.note: Ground beef costs less and is easier to find. Cook it the same way, to 160°F.
Chop gluten-free rolled oats fine and use the same amount.

steps.text: Peel the onion and cut it in half. Grate it on the large holes of the box grater into the large bowl.
steps.tip: Stop when the onion half gets small, and keep your fingertips clear of the holes.

steps.text: Tip the grated onion into the middle of the towel. Gather up the towel, twist it over the sink, and squeeze out as much juice as you can. Put the onion back in the bowl.
steps.look: A small, damp clump of onion, with no juice dripping.

steps.text: Chop the parsley fine. Peel the garlic and chop it as small as you can. Add both to the onion.

Add the lamb, panko, cumin, paprika, cinnamon, the kofta's salt, and the pepper. Mix and squeeze it all together with your hands for about 2 minutes, until it's one sticky mass. Then wet your hands with cold water, divide the mixture into 18 pieces about the size of an egg, and roll each into a log about 3 inches long. Lay them on the plate.
steps.look: The mixture sticks to itself and pulls away from the bowl in one piece.
steps.tip: Wet your hands again every few logs, so the meat doesn't stick.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw lamb or its package touched.
Chop the mint. In the small bowl, stir together the yogurt, mint, lemon juice, and the sauce's salt. Put it in the fridge.
Slice the cucumber and tomatoes into thin rounds.
Heat the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Use the tongs to lay the kofta in the pan with space between them, laying each one down away from you.
Wash the tongs in hot, soapy water, and wash your hands. Put the raw-lamb plate in the sink.
Cook the kofta, turning them a quarter turn with the tongs every 2 minutes, until they're brown on every side.
steps.look: A deep brown crust all the way around.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the end of the thickest kofta, so the tip is in the middle. It needs to read at least 160°F. If it doesn't, cook 2 more minutes and check again.
Turn off the stove and move the kofta to a clean plate. Wrap the pitas in a damp paper towel and microwave them until warm.
steps.tip: The steam inside is hot. Open the paper towel slowly.

steps.text: Lay 3 kofta in each pita with cucumber and tomato, and spoon the yogurt sauce over the top.

grate.text: Peel the onion and halve it through the root. Grate it on the large holes of the box grater into the large bowl, stopping when you're down to the root end.

squeeze.text: Tip the onion into the towel, twist it closed over the sink, and squeeze until no more juice drips. Put the onion back in the bowl.
squeeze.look: A damp, compact clump, with no liquid pooling under it.

herbs.text: Dry the parsley well and chop it fine, to about ⅛ inch. Peel and mince the garlic. Add both to the onion.

mix-shape.text: Add the lamb, panko, cumin, paprika, cinnamon, the kofta's salt, and the pepper, and knead it all with your hands for 2 minutes, until sticky. Pinch off 1 tablespoon and flatten it into a test patty. With wet hands, divide the rest into 18 even pieces and roll each into a log 3 inches long and 1 inch thick. Lay the test patty and the logs on the plate.
mix-shape.look: Every log about the same size, with no cracks.

wash-shape.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wipe the counter, the bowl's rim, and anything the raw lamb or its package touched.

sauce.text: Chop the mint fine. In the small bowl, stir together the yogurt, mint, lemon juice, and the sauce's salt, and refrigerate it.

veg.text: Slice the cucumber and tomatoes into ¼-inch rounds.

add.text: Lay the kofta in the pan with the clean tongs, 1 inch apart, laying each one down away from you. If they don't all fit, cook them in two batches.

wash-add.text: Wash the tongs and your hands. Put the raw-lamb plate in the sink and set out a clean plate for the cooked kofta.

brown.text: Cook the kofta, turning each a quarter turn every 2 minutes, until browned on all four sides.
brown.look: An even, deep brown crust all the way around.

check.text: Check the three thickest kofta: slide the thermometer in from one end so the tip is in the middle. Each needs at least 160°F. Move the ones that are done to the clean plate, and give the rest 1 more minute before checking again.

pita.text: Turn off the stove. Wrap the pitas in a damp paper towel and microwave them until warm and soft.

serve.text: Fill each pita with 3 kofta, cucumber, and tomato, and spoon the yogurt sauce over.

add.text: Lay the test patty in the pan with the tongs.
Wash the tongs in hot, soapy water and dry them.
Cook the test patty 2 minutes a side, turning it with the spatula. Check it from the side with the thermometer: 160°F. Taste it, and if it needs it, sprinkle a little more salt over the shaped logs.

move.title: Shape it, then prove it's done
move.body: Kofta are logs of spiced ground lamb, cooked across Lebanon, Syria, and Turkey. This week's skill is the thermometer: ground meat is only safe once its middle reaches 160°F, and you can't see that from the outside. You'll cook a small test patty to check the seasoning, brown the kofta on every side, and check the middle of the thickest ones before anything comes off the heat.

wrong.sign: The kofta fall apart in the pan
wrong.fix: The mixture was too wet or not mixed enough. Knead what's left a little longer with a spoonful more panko.

wrong.sign: The outside is dark but the middle reads under 160°F
wrong.fix: Turn the heat to medium and cook 2 minutes more, turning them, before checking again. Next batch, start a little lower.

wrong.sign: Two kofta read very different temperatures
wrong.fix: They aren't the same size. Keep cooking the ones under 160°F and take the rest out; next time, weigh or measure the pieces so they match.
Sprinkle a little more salt over the shaped logs, or knead a pinch more cumin into them, before they cook.

quiz.q: Why does ground lamb need 160°F when a lamb chop is safe at 145°F?
choices: Grinding mixes surface bacteria all the way through
quiz.explain: In a whole cut, the inside was never exposed. In ground meat, it was.

quiz.q: Where does the thermometer go in a kofta?
choices: In from one end, tip in the middle
quiz.explain: From the top, the tip can pass through into the pan.

choices: To taste the seasoning while you can still change it
quiz.explain: You can't taste raw meat, so you taste a cooked spoonful.

choices: The thickest ones, since they're the last to reach 160°F
Only the first one in the pan
Any one, they're all the same
quiz.explain: If the thickest are done, the thinner ones are too.

add.title: Why ground lamb needs 160°F
add.body: Bacteria live on the surface of meat. A whole lamb chop seared hard is safe at 145°F because its inside was never exposed. Grinding mixes the surface all the way through, so every part of a kofta has to reach 160°F, the middle included.

add.title: A test patty
add.body: You can't taste raw meat, so cooks fry a spoonful first. It tells you whether the mixture needs more salt or spice while you can still fix it, and it's a quick practice run with the thermometer on something thin.

add.title: Go in from the end
add.body: The tip of the thermometer is where it reads. A kofta is only about an inch thick, so a probe pushed in from the top hits the pan. Slide it in from one end, along the length, so the tip sits in the middle, the last part to get hot.
